title: Encrypt the tax-id column so a changed row is refused

blocks.text: The customers table keeps each customer's tax id encrypted, one byte array per row in a single column. Several instances of the service share one AES key from the key store, and the nightly export job reads the column with the same key. Support staff can edit rows directly in the database.
Finish `seal` and `open` in `src/main/java/practice/ColumnCipher.java`. When you're done:

items: whatever `seal` returns is all that is stored, and any `ColumnCipher` with the same key opens it back into the same tax id;
the same tax id sealed twice is never stored with the same IV;
a stored value that was changed in the database is refused with a `GeneralSecurityException` (or a subclass), never returned as a tax id.

blocks.text: The tests use their own key, generated when they start, and a `new SecureRandom()`. About fifteen lines in total.

cases.says: every tax id, the empty one and a long one included, opens back into itself
a stored value with one byte changed is refused with a GeneralSecurityException instead of decrypting to a different tax id
sealing the same tax id six times on one instance gives six different IVs and six different stored values
a second instance with the same key opens values the first one sealed, in any order, so the stored value carries its own IV

origin.section: A GCM IV Used Twice Under One Key Gives Away the XOR of the Two Plaintexts

concepts: AES-GCM stores a 12-byte IV in front of the ciphertext and a 16-byte tag after it, and decryption throws AEADBadTagException for any changed byte; a mode without a tag, such as CTR, decrypts a changed ciphertext into changed plaintext.
Two GCM encryptions under the same key and IV share a keystream, so their ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of the plaintexts; each encryption needs its own IV, stored with the ciphertext.
